hints.junior: Deleting one feature meant hunting through components/, hooks/, utils/, and services/ separately, no folder said "this is everything."
hints.mid: Layer folders group by what kind of code it is, not what it's for, so every feature ends up smeared across all four.
hints.staff: Layer folders give no structural signal about coupling, nothing stops an unrelated feature quietly importing a "util" that was never really shared.

hints.junior: Same eight files, two trees, toggle to see what it takes to find and delete one feature's worth of them.
hints.mid: Only the grouping differs between the two trees, the files themselves are identical.
hints.staff: In the layer tree, unrelated features sit beside saved-searches in every folder with nothing hinting they don't belong together.

hints.junior: A feature folder holds that feature's component, hook, and util together, deleting the feature means deleting one folder.
hints.mid: Shared components/ and utils/ still exist, but only for things genuinely used by more than one feature.
hints.staff: Real feature-sliced conventions restrict cross-slice imports to a public entry point, turning the convention into something a lint rule can check.

hints.junior: If only one feature uses something today, it starts in that feature's folder, it moves to shared only once a second feature needs it.
hints.mid: A feature-sliced structure earns its value most at deletion or hand-off time, not during day-to-day authoring, which gets a small added tax.
hints.staff: Without an enforced import boundary, feature folders degrade back into the same coupling over time, just with different folder names.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about deleting one feature and having to hunt through four different folders just to find everything it owns.
sections.mid: Organizing by technical layer groups files by what kind of code they are, not what they're for — every feature ends up with its code smeared across all four folders.
sections.staff: The deeper cost isn't navigation friction, it's that layer-based folders provide no structural signal about coupling — nothing stops an unrelated feature from importing a util that never expressed which feature it belonged to.

sections.junior: The fix is grouping files by what they're for instead of what type of file they are, so one feature's code lives in one folder.
sections.mid: The organizing question flips from what type of file is this to what does this belong to — a shared folder still exists, but reserved for things genuinely used by more than one feature.
sections.staff: A real feature-sliced convention typically enforces that other slices can only import from a feature's public entry point, not reach into its internals directly, turning an informal convention into something a lint rule can check.

sections.junior: Toggle between a layer based tree and a feature based tree, and see what it takes to find and delete one feature in each.
sections.mid: The same eight files exist in both trees — only their grouping differs, one by file type, the other by feature.
sections.staff: In the layer tree, unrelated features' files sit directly beside each other in every folder — there's no boundary that would even hint one doesn't belong with the others.

sections.junior: Group your files by feature, not by file type. It makes deleting or handing off a feature a one folder operation instead of a scavenger hunt.
sections.mid: Reserve shared folders for code genuinely used by more than one feature — a single-caller helper starts inside that feature's own folder.
sections.staff: Enforce the slice boundary with a lint rule restricting cross-feature imports to a public entry point, or feature folders degrade back into the same coupling.
